explainer.heading: What the poem says
explainer.body: W. H. Davies asks what life is worth if, full of worries, we have no time to stand and stare. He lists the simple joys we miss: standing beneath the boughs and staring as long as sheep or cows; seeing where squirrels hide nuts in grass; seeing streams full of sunlight sparkling like stars at night; turning at Beauty’s glance and watching her dance and smile. He ends: it is a poor life if we have no time to stand and stare.
explainer.example: Theme: slow down and enjoy nature and simple pleasures.
explainer.hook: Opening and closing couplets almost the same.

explainer.heading: Imagery
explainer.body: Nature images: boughs, sheep and cows, woods, squirrels hiding nuts, “streams full of stars, like skies at night” (sunlight glittering on water). Beauty is personified as a woman whose glance, dancing feet and smile we have no time to notice.

explainer.heading: Rhetorical question
explainer.body: A question asked to make a point, not to get an answer. “What is this life if, full of care, / We have no time to stand and stare?” really means: such a life is not worth much.
explainer.example: Another: “No time to wait till her mouth can / Enrich that smile her eyes began?”

explainer.heading: Other devices
explainer.body: Simile: “Streams full of stars, like skies at night”. Repetition / anaphora: “No time to…” begins many lines. Rhyming couplets: care/stare, boughs/cows, pass/grass, daylight/night, glance/dance, can/began.

explainer.heading: The poet
explainer.body: William Henry Davies was a Welsh poet of the Georgian poetry movement, born in 1871 in Monmouthshire. He spent much of his life as a tramp, travelling through the USA and the UK; his attitude to life shows in “Leisure”.

questions.q: Pick out two things from nature that, according to the poet, we have no time to see.
questions.model: We have no time to see where squirrels hide their nuts in grass, and no time to see streams full of sunlight sparkling like stars. (Also: standing beneath boughs like sheep or cows.)

questions.q: What does the poet say about modern life in “Leisure”? How does he use the rhetorical question to make his point?
questions.model: The poet says people are so full of worries and busy that they have no time to stand and stare at nature — trees, cattle, squirrels, sparkling streams — or to notice beauty. Such a life is poor. He opens with a rhetorical question, “What is this life if, full of care, / We have no time to stand and stare?”, which does not expect an answer but suggests that such a life has little value. He repeats “No time to…” and ends with “A poor life this if…”, stressing the need to slow down and enjoy simple pleasures.
points: Busy, worried life; no time to enjoy nature/beauty
Rhetorical question explained (no answer expected; makes a point)
Message: slow down; repetition/ending reinforces it
